articles.title: Why a Banner Tracker Needs an Evidence-State Model
articles.excerpt: Live-service game guides have a difficult data problem: the most searched question is often the least stable one. A player wants to know the current banner, what comes next, and when the phase changes…
articles.body: Live-service game guides have a difficult data problem: the most searched question is often the least stable one. A player wants to know the current banner, what comes next, and when the phase changes. Those answers can become wrong within hours, while community speculation can look almost identical to confirmed information in a feed. I approached this as a state-modeling problem rather than a stream of blog posts. The key is to store what is known , how it is known , and when the snapshot was rebuilt as separate fields.

articles.body: In October 2026 we applied for TikTok's Content Posting API for a scheduling tool we used for our own small media brands. TikTok rejected it on 12 October: tools for personal or internal company use are not eligible, and the site said "not open for public sign-up". We had two options: give up on TikTok scheduling, or build a product anyone can use. We picked the second. Ten days later, on 22 October, TikTok approved it. What ViralGenHub is A social media scheduler with a calendar, per-platform previews, a media library, saved templates (Sets) and Signatures. Platforms available today: TikTok, Bluesky, Mastodon, LinkedIn (profiles), Tumblr, Discord, Slack, Telegram, Kick, Dribbble, WordPress, Listmonk, dev.to, Nostr and Lemmy.

articles.body: When you post to six networks at once, "it worked" and "it failed" are the rare cases. The common one is: it worked on five, and one network said no. Maybe a token expired. Maybe the caption was too long for that one network. Maybe the network was having a bad minute. The problem: it looked like success In early versions of Clienzo, such a post was marked Published, because most of it was. The one failure sat inside it, visible only if you opened that post. People did not open it. Why would they? It said Published.

articles.title: Slow Websites Cost Revenue: A Performance Guide
articles.excerpt: Developers talk about load time in milliseconds. Business owners talk about it in revenue. This post bridges the two: a performance-budget approach to the same math — how to translate LCP, INP, and CL…
articles.body: Developers talk about load time in milliseconds. Business owners talk about it in revenue. This post bridges the two: a performance-budget approach to the same math — how to translate LCP, INP, and CLS into a conversion argument your clients (or your boss) will actually act on. Do the revenue math first Performance work is easier to approve when it is priced. Use this formula: Monthly visitors × conversion-rate improvement × average order value = monthly revenue gain. Take an illustrative scenario, not a promise: a site with 10,000 monthly visitors lifts its conversion rate from 2% to 2.2%. That 0.2-percentage-point gain means 20 extra conversions per month. At a $100 average order value, that is $2,000 per month, or $24,000 over a year if the improvement holds. Your numbers will differ.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 25, 1671: Astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovers Iapetus, Saturn's 'yin-yang' moon
articles.excerpt: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Oct. 25, 1671, the Italian astronomer Giovanni Cassini discovered a new moon at Saturn! Iapetus was the second moon anyone had ever found orbiting Saturn, and it was the first of four moons Cassini would discover at the ringed planet. The Dutch astronomer Christiaan Huygens had discovered Titan , the largest of Saturn's moons, about six years earlier. After Cassini found Iapetus, he also found the moons Rhea, Tethys and Dione. When Cassini first saw Iapetus, the moon looked like a tiny speck on the west side of Saturn. He calculated its orbit and thought he would be able to see it again on the east side of Saturn 39 days later, but it was nowhere to be seen.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 24, 1946: V-2 rocket takes 1st photos of Earth from space
articles.excerpt: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On October 24, 1946, a V-2 rocket captured the first-ever photo of Earth from space. While these grainy, black-and-white images might not look like much today, they were a huge deal at the time, because no one had ever seen Earth from space before. The V-2 rocket launched from the White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico. It carried a 35-millimeter motion picture camera that captured a new frame every second and a half. The rocket soared to an altitude of about 65 miles before falling back to Earth. Both the rocket and the camera were destroyed after crashing into the Earth at a speed of about 340 miles per hour. But the film survived because it was protected inside a steel case. Scientists had to drive out into the New Mexico desert to retrieve the film.

articles.title: 'Star Trek: Strange New Worlds' was afraid to say anything in season of gimmicks
articles.excerpt: The fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was one giant gimmick: shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres.
articles.body: It didn’t take long for fans to figure out that the fourth season of "Star Trek: Strange New Worlds" was going to be unlike any season of " Star Trek " before it. The entire season was one giant gimmick, and that gimmick was shoving "Trek" into as many genres as possible and often directly adapting classic films from those genres. You could argue that an entire season of gimmick episodes is a bold risk: putting the characters in fun, wacky situations to see how they react. It could be interesting, but the season we got never made the most of the concept. It was all so safe and paint-by-numbers, and, most importantly, it didn't have anything profound or interesting to say. That should trouble any Trekkie.

Over millennia, the night sky has helped shape human beliefs.
